item.title: Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1 (Whistler’s Mother)
item.lesson: The world calls it Whistler's Mother; Whistler insisted on Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, and the gap between those titles is a whole theory of art. The American expatriate — Paris-trained, London-based, dandy, duelist of wits — argued that painting should work like music: 'arrangements' and 'nocturnes' of tone and shape, valuable for their composition rather than their story. 'To me it is interesting as a picture of my mother,' he allowed, 'but what can or ought the public to care about the identity of the portrait?' The public overruled him. Anna McNeill Whistler, sitting in profile in Puritan black (she posed when a model failed to appear), became the century's great icon of stern maternal devotion — a reading that ignores every word of the painter's manifesto. Both are right: it is a radically austere formal design, gray on gray on black, and it is somebody's mother. France bought it in 1891, the first American painting to enter the national collection — the ultimate validation for an artist his homeland had barely claimed.
item.lookFor: Count what Whistler permits himself: one curtain, one framed print, one profile, a floor line. Then notice how the black mass of her dress is held in place by the pale rectangle of her face and cap — the 'arrangement' doing exactly what he said it did.
